label: thm:main
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:private
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The reverse implication in~\eqref{eq:rigidity} follows from
idempotent addition. Suppose that the inequality holds. If $m$
contained a variable outside $\bigcup\mathcal E$, assigning that variable
$\infty$ and all other variables $1$ would give $m=\infty$ and
$p_{\mathcal E}=1$, a contradiction. Thus $\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq\bigcup\mathcal E$.

Choose one point $z_E\in D_E$ independently for each $E\in\mathcal E$.
Assign $a$ to the chosen points and $1$ to all other variables.
Every monomial $m_E$ has value $a$, so $p_{\mathcal E}=a$ and the assumed
inequality forces $m=a$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:private-exponents}
\sum_{E\in\mathcal E}\operatorname{occ}(z_E,m)=1
\end{equation}
for every such choice. Varying $z_E$ with the other choices fixed
shows that the exponent of each point of $D_E$ is a common
nonnegative integer $\alpha_E$. By~\eqref{eq:private-exponents},
$\sum_{E\in\mathcal E}\alpha_E=1$. Hence there is a unique $E_*\in\mathcal E$
with $\alpha_{E_*}=1$, and all other $\alpha_E$ are zero.

Now let $x\in\bigcup\mathcal E$ be a point that is not private to any
member. Take $x$, together with one private point from each member
not containing $x$. This is an exact transversal. Assigning $a$ to
it and $1$ elsewhere gives
\[
\operatorname{occ}(x,m)+\sum_{\substack{E\in\mathcal E\\x\notin E}}\alpha_E=1.
\]
It follows that $\operatorname{occ}(x,m)=1$ if $x\in E_*$ and is zero otherwise.
Together with the exponents on the private points, this proves
$m=m_{E_*}$.

For the last assertion, the same construction works for any
$x\in\bigcup\mathcal E$, whether or not it is private: take $x$ and one
private point from each member not containing it.

label: lem:stability
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the assertion for one replacement inside a fixed
multiplicative context. Let $f\approx g$ be an identity of $S_7$
in at most $n$ variables, let $\phi$ be an arbitrary substitution,
and let $l,r\in X^*$. Suppose that $l\phi(f)r$ is supported by
$\mathcal F$. Put $c=\operatorname{cm}(lr)$. We shall prove that $l\phi(g)r$ is also
supported by $\mathcal F$.

The two sides of any identity of $S_7$ have the same variable
content. Indeed, assigning $\infty$ to a variable occurring on only
one side and $1$ to all others gives values $\infty$ and $1$.
Let $y_1,\ldots,y_d$, with $d\leq n$, be this common content.

Every word in $\operatorname{Wd}(f)$ is linear. Otherwise some $y_i$ occurs
twice in such a word. Choosing the same nonempty word from
$\operatorname{Wd}(\phi(y_i))$ at those occurrences, and choosing arbitrary
words at the remaining occurrences, produces a non-linear word
in $\operatorname{Wd}(l\phi(f)r)$, a contradiction. In particular, $f$ has at
most $2^d-1\leq2^n-1$ distinct commutative images of words.

Fix one commutative monomial $m_i$ of $\operatorname{cm}(\phi(y_i))$ for each
$i$. All monomials of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-substitution}
c\,\operatorname{cm}(f)(m_1,\ldots,m_d)
\end{equation}
are squarefree and correspond to members of $\mathcal F$. Their distinct
supports form a nonempty subfamily $\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal F$ with
$|\mathcal E|\leq2^n-1$. For every $E\in\mathcal E$,
\[
\left|E\cap\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal E\setminus\{E\}}F\right|
\leq(|\mathcal E|-1)\ell\leq(2^n-2)\ell<k\leq|E|.
\]
Thus every member of $\mathcal E$ has a private point. This observation
holds for every fixed choice of the monomials $m_i$.

We next show that every word in $\operatorname{Wd}(g)$ is linear. For this
purpose keep the current choice of the $m_i$. Fix $i$ and take
$z\in\operatorname{supp}(m_i)$, which is possible because substitution words
are nonempty. Since $y_i$ occurs in $f$, the product $cm_i$
divides a squarefree monomial in~\eqref{eq:fixed-substitution}.
Hence $z\notin\operatorname{supp}(c)$, and $m_i$ is squarefree.

There is an exact transversal $Z$ of $\mathcal E$ that contains $z$ and
avoids $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. If $\mathcal E$ has one member, take $Z=\{z\}$.
Otherwise $\operatorname{supp}(c)$ is contained in every member of $\mathcal E$, so
no private point belongs to $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. The construction at the
end of Lemma~\ref{lem:private} then gives the required $Z$.
Assign $a$ to variables in $Z$ and $1$ to all other variables.
Under this evaluation $c=1$ and every monomial
in~\eqref{eq:fixed-substitution} has value $a$.
Each $m_j$ divides at least one of these squarefree monomials,
so its value lies in $\{1,a\}$; the value of $m_i$ is $a$.

The values of the $m_j$ therefore define an assignment of
$y_1,\ldots,y_d$ under which $f=a$ and $y_i=a$. Since
$S_7\models f\approx g$, this assignment also gives $g=a$.
If any word of $g$ repeated $y_i$, its value would be $\infty$,
and consequently $g$ would have value $\infty$. This is
impossible. Applying this argument for each $i$ proves that all
words of $g$ are linear.

Now take an arbitrary word in $\operatorname{Wd}(l\phi(g)r)$, and let $m$ be
its commutative image. It comes from a word $v\in\operatorname{Wd}(g)$ and
choices of words at its variable occurrences. Since $v$ is
linear, these choices give one monomial $m_i$ for each variable
appearing in $v$; choose $m_i$ arbitrarily for the other variables.
Thus
\[
m=c\,\operatorname{cm}(v)(m_1,\ldots,m_d).
\]
With this new fixed choice, the monomials of
$c\,\operatorname{cm}(f)(m_1,\ldots,m_d)$ again form $p_{\mathcal E}$ for a
subfamily $\mathcal E$ having a private point in every member. Because
$v$ is a summand of $g$ and $S_7\models f\approx g$, we have
$S_7\models v\preccurlyeq f$. Substitution and multiplication
by the context give
\[
S_7\models
c\,\operatorname{cm}(v)(m_1,\ldots,m_d)
\preccurlyeq
c\,\operatorname{cm}(f)(m_1,\ldots,m_d)=p_{\mathcal E}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:private} implies that $m=m_E$ for some
$E\in\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal F$. This proves the assertion for the fixed
multiplicative context.

Finally, a term context with a single occurrence of a placeholder
$z$ expands as
\[
h+\sum_{j=1}^s l_jzr_j,
\]
where $s\geq1$, $l_j,r_j\in X^*$, and $h$ may be absent.
This follows by induction on the context using distributivity.
If the old expanded term is supported by $\mathcal F$, every word in
each $l_j\phi(f)r_j$ has that property. The argument above
applies to each $j$, and the summands of $h$ are unchanged.
It also applies with $f$ and $g$ interchanged. The ai-semiring
axioms preserve expanded word sets by~\eqref{eq:expansion}.
Induction on a sequence of equational replacements proves the
lemma.

label: rem:stability
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:stability}
The members of $\mathcal F$ need not have equal sizes. Moreover, the
proof permits arbitrary polynomial substitutions. The argument
establishing linearity of $g$ is what allows each output word to
be represented by a consistent choice of one substitution word
for each source variable.

label: lem:semilinear
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The language $L_b$ is recognized by a finite automaton whose
states are a new initial state $*$ and the elements of $S$.
Reading $s_i$ at $*$ leads to $s_i$, and reading $s_i$ at a
state $t\in S$ leads to $ts_i$. The only accepting state is
$b$. The initial state is separate even when $S$ has an
identity, so the empty word is not accepted.

For completeness, a finite automaton yields a regular expression
by eliminating states. If $R_{ij}^{(h)}$ denotes an expression
for paths from state $i$ to state $j$ whose intermediate states
are among the first $h$ states, then
\[
R_{ij}^{(h)}=R_{ij}^{(h-1)}\cup
R_{ih}^{(h-1)}\bigl(R_{hh}^{(h-1)}\bigr)^*R_{hj}^{(h-1)}.
\]
Start with the direct transition labels and include the empty
word when $i=j$. This gives a finite regular expression for
$L_b$.

Parikh vectors turn concatenation into vector addition.
Semilinear sets are closed under finite unions and setwise
addition. They are also closed under the additive star, the
operation taking all finite sums of elements, including the
empty sum. Indeed, if
$A=\bigcup_{i=1}^h(\mathbf b_i+\mathbb N V_i)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:star}
A^*=\bigcup_{I\subseteq[h]}
\left(
\sum_{i\in I}\mathbf b_i+
\mathbb N\left(\{\mathbf b_i:i\in I\}\cup\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i\right)
\right).
\end{equation}
The summand for $I=\varnothing$ is $\{\mathbf 0\}$. To verify
the formula, let $I$ record the linear components used at least
once in a finite sum. Their first base vectors give
$\sum_{i\in I}\mathbf b_i$, and further base vectors and all
period vectors give the indicated nonnegative combinations.
Conversely, any such combination can be realized by using
component $i$ once plus as many additional times as its base
vector requires, and placing all its period vectors in one
of those occurrences.

The Parikh images of the atomic regular expressions are
semilinear. Induction on a regular expression, using the three
closure properties just proved, shows that $P_b$ is semilinear.
There are finitely many $b\in S$ and finitely many components
in their chosen representations. Taking the maximum of their
quantities in~\eqref{eq:B}, and of $1$, gives the required $B$.

label: lem:probability
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:rounding
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $b=\nu(1)\cdots\nu(N)$, and let
$\mathbf N=(N_1,\ldots,N_r)$ be the count vector of the assignment.
Then $\mathbf N\in P_b$, so it belongs to one of the chosen
linear components:
\[
\mathbf N=\mathbf b+\sum_{j=1}^q n_j\mathbf v_j.
\]
Put $\alpha=L/N\leq1$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rounding}
\mathbf M=\mathbf b+\sum_{j=1}^q\lfloor\alpha n_j\rfloor\mathbf v_j.
\end{equation}
Since $0\leq\lfloor\alpha n_j\rfloor\leq n_j$, we have
$\mathbf 0\leq\mathbf M\leq\mathbf N$ coordinatewise. Moreover,
$\mathbf M\in P_b$ and
\begin{align*}
\lVert \mathbf M-\alpha\mathbf N\rVert_1
&\leq(1-\alpha)\lVert \mathbf b\rVert_1
  +\sum_{j=1}^q\lVert \mathbf v_j\rVert_1\\
&\leq B.
\end{align*}
Because $\lVert \alpha\mathbf N\rVert_1=L$, the integer
$s=\lVert \mathbf M\rVert_1$ lies between $k=L-B$ and $K=L+B$.

There is a word over $S$ with count vector $\mathbf M$ and product
$b$. Any set of positions with exactly $M_i$ occurrences of
$s_i$ can be ordered to spell this word: match its occurrences
of each letter to the chosen positions with that value.
Thus every set with count vector $\mathbf M$ realizes the full
product. Conditional on $|E|=s$, the probability that $E$
has exactly this count vector is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hypergeometric}
\frac{\prod_{i=1}^r\binom{N_i}{M_i}}{\binom Ns}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, this expression is a lower bound for the
conditional probability that $E$ realizes the full product.

Call an index $i$ rare if $N_i<N/(2L)$. The bound on the
rounding error gives
\[
M_i\leq\alpha N_i+B<B+\tfrac12
\]
for every rare $i$. Hence $M_i\leq B$, and the number of
selected positions with rare values is
$d=\sum_{i\text{ rare}}M_i\leq rB=C$.
For a nonrare $i$, the hypothesis $N\geq4LK$ implies
\mbox{$N_i\geq2K\geq2M_i$}. Consequently,
\[
\binom{N_i}{M_i}
=\frac{N_i(N_i-1)\cdots(N_i-M_i+1)}{M_i!}
\geq\frac{(N/(4L))^{M_i}}{M_i!},
\]
with the usual value $1$ when $M_i=0$.
For rare indices use $\binom{N_i}{M_i}\geq1$.
Together with $\binom Ns\leq N^s$, this bounds
\eqref{eq:hypergeometric} below by
\[
\frac{N^{s-d}}{(4L)^{s-d}(K!)^rN^s}
\geq (4L)^{-K}(K!)^{-r}N^{-C}.
\]
Finally, the probability of choosing the size $s$ is
$1/(2B+1)$. This proves~\eqref{eq:probability}.

label: lem:cover
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:choose-k
title: Proof
body_md:
Use $r$, $B$ and $C=rB$ as above. Choose, in this order,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:choose-k}
t=2C+3,\qquad \ell=t-1,\qquad
k=\max\{t,(2^n-2)(t-1)+1\}.
\end{equation}
Let $L,K,c$ be as in~\eqref{eq:constants}, and put
\[
A=\frac{\log r+2}{c},\qquad
M=\lceil AN^{C+1}\rceil.
\]
Independently sample $M$ sets using the distribution in
Lemma~\ref{lem:probability}.

For a fixed assignment $\nu$, the probability that no sampled
set realizes its full product is at most
\[
(1-cN^{-C})^M\leq \exp(-cN^{-C}M)
\leq\exp(-cAN).
\]
There are $r^N$ assignments. The union bound therefore shows
that the probability that condition~\textup{(iii)} fails is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coverage-failure}
r^N\exp(-cAN)=\exp(-2N).
\end{equation}

We also estimate intersections of two independently sampled
sets $E$ and $F$. Given $E$ and $|F|=s$, for a fixed
$t$-element subset $T\subseteq E$,
\[
\Pr(T\subseteq F\mid E,|F|=s)
=\frac{\binom{N-t}{s-t}}{\binom Ns}
\leq\left(\frac{K}{N-t+1}\right)^t.
\]
Since $|E|\leq K$, another union bound, followed by averaging
over the sizes, gives for $N\geq2t$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-failure}
\Pr(|E\cap F|\geq t)\leq b_0N^{-t},
\qquad b_0=\binom Kt(2K)^t.
\end{equation}
It follows that the probability of any pair of sampled sets
having intersection of size at least $t$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-pairs-failure}
\binom M2 b_0N^{-t}
\leq \frac{b_0(A+1)^2}{2N},
\end{equation}
where we used $M\leq(A+1)N^{C+1}$ and $t=2C+3$.

The quantities $r,B,C,t,\ell,k,L,K,c,A,b_0$ are independent
of $N$. Choose an integer $N$ with
\[
N\geq\max\{4LK,2t,K+1,2\},\qquad N>b_0(A+1)^2.
\]
Then~\eqref{eq:coverage-failure} and
\eqref{eq:all-pairs-failure} are each less than $1/2$.
With positive probability neither failure occurs. The resulting
sets are all distinct: a repeated set would have intersection
at least $k\geq t$ with its other occurrence. Taking them as
$\mathcal F$ proves~\textup{(i)} and~\textup{(iii)}, and the choices
in~\eqref{eq:choose-k} give~\textup{(ii)}.

label: rem:order
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:order}
Semilinearity gives a short count vector representing the same
product, but does not preserve the original order of the selected
positions. Accordingly, condition~\textup{(iii)} allows all
orderings of a member of $\mathcal F$. Also, the interval of permitted
sizes $[k,k+2B]$ accommodates the rounding error in
\eqref{eq:rounding}; an exact prescribed size is not required.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, to the contrary, that $R$ has a finite identity basis
$\Sigma$ relative to the ai-semiring axioms. Choose $n\geq1$
at least as large as the number of variables in any identity of
$\Sigma$. Since $S_7\in\mathsf V(R)$, every identity of $R$ holds
in $S_7$, and therefore
\[
\Sigma\subseteq\operatorname{Id}_n(S_7).
\]

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} to the multiplicative semigroup
$(R,\cdot)$ and to $n$. Identify a position $i\in[N]$ with a
distinct variable $x_i$, and use the same notation $\mathcal F$ for
the resulting family of sets of variables. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:obstruction}
P=\sum_{E\in\mathcal F}\ \sum_{u\in\operatorname{Sym}(E)}u,
\qquad w=x_1x_2\cdots x_N.
\end{equation}
For every assignment of these variables to $R$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:cover}\textup{(iii)} supplies a member $E$ and
an ordering of it whose product equals the value of $w$.
That ordering occurs as a summand of $P$. Idempotent addition
then gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:witness}
R\models P+w\approx P.
\end{equation}

The term $P$ is supported by $\mathcal F$. The intersection and size
conditions in Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} are exactly the hypotheses
of Lemma~\ref{lem:stability}. Thus every term equated to $P$
using $\Sigma$ and the ai-semiring axioms must also be
supported by $\mathcal F$. However, $P+w$ has the word $w$ with
support of size $N>K$. This support is not a member of $\mathcal F$.
Hence~\eqref{eq:witness} cannot follow from $\Sigma$,
contradicting that $\Sigma$ is an identity basis of $R$.
head: environment

label: cor:separation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:separation}
For every finite ai-semiring $R$ and every $n\geq1$, there is
an identity of $R$ that is not a consequence of
$\operatorname{Id}_n(S_7)$ together with the ai-semiring axioms.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Construct $P$ and $w$ from the multiplicative semigroup of $R$
as in~\eqref{eq:obstruction}. The identity $P+w\approx P$
holds in $R$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cover}, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:stability} excludes its derivation from
$\operatorname{Id}_n(S_7)$.

label: prop:upward
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $T$ is finite and $A\in\mathsf V(T)$, then
$S_7\in\mathsf V(A)\subseteq\mathsf V(T)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:main},
$T$ is nonfinitely based, as required.

label: prop:powers
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:powers}
Let $A$ be a finite ai-semiring. The map
\[
\pi:\mathcal P^+(A,\cdot)\longrightarrow A,
\qquad U\longmapsto\sum_{a\in U}a
\]
is a surjective homomorphism. Consequently, if
$S_7\in\mathsf V(A)$, both $\mathcal P^+(A,\cdot)$ and
$\mathcal P(A,\cdot)$ are strongly nonfinitely based.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map is surjective because $\pi(\{a\})=a$.
Associativity, commutativity and idempotence of addition give
$\pi(U\cup V)=\pi(U)+\pi(V)$. Distributivity and idempotence
give
\[
\pi(U)\pi(V)=\sum_{u\in U,\ v\in V}uv
=\sum_{b\in UV}b=\pi(UV).
\]
It follows that
\[
A\in\mathsf V\bigl(\mathcal P^+(A,\cdot)\bigr)
\subseteq\mathsf V\bigl(\mathcal P(A,\cdot)\bigr).
\]
Both power semirings are finite, so the conclusion follows
from Proposition~\ref{prop:upward}.
head: environment

label: cor:s7powers
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:powers} with $A=S_7$.

label: cor:groups
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e$ be the identity of $G$, and put $D=G\setminus\{e\}$.
We claim that $D^2=G$. Given $g\in G$, choose
$x\in G\setminus\{e,g\}$, which is possible since $|G|\geq3$.
Then $x\in D$ and $x^{-1}g\in D$, so
$g=x(x^{-1}g)\in D^2$.

The three distinct nonempty sets $\{e\}$, $D$ and $G$ form a
subsemiring of $\mathcal P^+(G)$. Their union of any two distinct
members is $G$. Setwise multiplication has identity $\{e\}$,
satisfies $D^2=G$, and has $G$ as an absorbing element on
this three-element subsemiring. Thus
\[
1\longmapsto\{e\},\qquad a\longmapsto D,
\qquad\infty\longmapsto G
\]
is an embedding of $S_7$. Proposition~\ref{prop:upward}
applies to both $\mathcal P^+(G)$ and $\mathcal P(G)$.
